title: Operational Trust: Messaging & Incident Narratives for Degradation
body:
Purpose:
This brief provides a concise, tactical messaging framework for GTM and CS to explain Redwood Inference's approach to reliability and graceful degradation. Audience: sales AE/SDRs, CS leads, solutions engineers, and product marketing creators who need short, defensible language and incident narratives to use in demos, proposals, and customer conversations.

High-level framing (one-liner options):
- Option A: "Redwood keeps apps functional — even under stress — by transparently degrading to safe, predictable fallbacks so customers never lose core product value."
- Option B: "When capacity or region issues occur, Redwood automatically routes and gracefully steps down to compatible models so user-facing features remain available and predictable."
- Option C (technical): "Smart routing + fallback model families + observability give predictable, measurable fallbacks with cost-aware policies."

Core messaging pillars (short hooks + supporting bullets):
1) Continuity-first design
   - Hook: "Designed to keep your user flows intact."
   - Support: automatic fallback chains, latency-preserving routing, and per-route policies that prioritize core features (auth, search, summarization) over low-value tokens.

2) Predictable degradation, not silent failure
   - Hook: "If we degrade, you’ll know what to expect."
   - Support: explicit, documentable fallbacks, token/latency SLAs with degradation profiles, and preview mode for degraded outputs in staging.

3) Measurable economics and tradeoffs
   - Hook: "Control cost vs. quality with observable levers."
   - Support: cost per token by path, quantization-aware model variants, and autoscaling policies tuned for unit economics.

4) Transparent incident communications (trust language)
   - Hook: "We surface the signal early and explain it clearly."
   - Support: SLO breach notifications, root-cause high-level narrative, and impact-scoped remediation timelines.

Incident narrative patterns (3 short stories sales/CS can use)
1) Regional capacity spike — retail flash sale
   - Scenario: East-coast region sees a sudden 8x request surge during a product drop.
   - What Redwood did: routed 40% of requests to adjacent region, applied short-duration quantized model variant for non-critical endpoints, and maintained core checkout chat and recommender features.
   - Outcome language for customers: "During the spike we rerouted and stepped certain routes down to a faster, smaller model for a brief window so checkout and recommendations stayed online with marginal quality impact. We’ll share exact latency and token-cost deltas post-incident."

2) Model regression discovered under load testing
   - Scenario: Canary shows a subtle quality regression in a newly onboarded model when sequence length > 1024 under sustained traffic.
   - What Redwood did: automatic canary rollback to previous model, active invocation of fallback family for long sequences, and gated rollout until regression is addressed.
   - Outcome language: "We detected the regression in our rollout pipeline and automatically rolled back the change; your traffic continued on the verified model family while we fixed the issue."

3) Cloud provider maintenance causes short region outage
   - Scenario: Provider performs network maintenance; small subset of instances return errors.
   - What Redwood did: switched to private routing over an alternate provider region for critical routes; noncritical routes entered degraded output mode with cached responses.
   - Outcome language: "We routed critical traffic through an alternate region and served cached/degraded responses for lower-priority paths; we then reconciled request logs and cost impact in the postmortem."

Competitive notes (short, differentiated claims)
- Competitor A (managed endpoints): 
   - Risk: black-box failover; customers often see opaque failures or large quality swings.
   - Redwood differentiation: explicit fallback chains, per-route degradation policies, and transparent SLO-era telemetry customers can inspect.

- Competitor B (self-hosted runtimes): 
   - Risk: customers must build routing/rollback/caching themselves.
   - Redwood differentiation: built-in routing + KV/prefix caching + rollout tooling removes engineering lift and reduces MTTD/MTTR.

- Competitor C (single-region focused providers): 
   - Risk: single-region dependencies limit availability.
   - Redwood differentiation: multi-region routing primitives and automatic, policy-driven region failovers with configurable latency/cost priorities.

Practical lines for reps (snappy)
- "We don’t only keep you online — we do it in ways you can audit and replicate."
- "When load or outages hit, we step down predictably so product value remains."
- "Fallbacks are first-class: they’re testable, versioned, and measurable."

Technical details reps should call out when prospects push back
- Policy-driven routing: route by latency, cost, or customer tier with automatic fallback to compatible model families.
- Degradation profiles: precomputed quality vs. latency/cost curves for each model variant so customers can pick acceptable tradeoffs.
- Observable rollback and canary tooling: automatic canary detection with immediate rollback and staged re-rollout after regression fixes.

Recommended collateral and short-form artifacts to produce
- One-pager: "Degradation guarantees and what they look like in-app" (visuals: flow showing routing → fallback → cached response).
- Demo script: show a simulated region spike where a feature continues to work under degraded quality.
- CS playbook: email templates, escalations, and customer postmortem summary template with cost/quality impact sections.

Risk/FAQ (prospect objections and suggested answers)
- Q: "If you route to other regions, what about data residency?"
  A: policy toggle — region failover can be disabled for regulated routes; we also support Private deployment with local-only routing for strict requirements.
- Q: "How bad is degraded output?"
  A: degradation profiles are explicit per route and per model variant; customers can preview degraded outputs in staging and set per-route thresholds.
- Q: "Does fallback hurt costs?"
  A: sometimes stepping down reduces GPU cost; in other cases, routing cross-region raises egress — we provide per-route cost deltas in the Console so customers can balance tradeoffs.

Call to action / next steps
- Create the one-pager (PM: Marissa Li) and demo script (SE lead: Evan Cho) by 2025-02-12.
- Build a short recording of the region-spike demo for enablement.
- Add the degradation profile visual to product tours and the pricing page.

Appendix: suggested postmortem template language (short)
- Executive summary: what happened, how many customers were impacted, duration.
- Action taken: immediate fallbacks invoked, rollbacks, region routing, and mitigation steps.
- Customer impact statement: features affected and expected quality delta.
- Follow-ups: remediation, changelog, and preventive items.

Notes and references:
- Aligns to internal ops playbook: confluence.redwood.ai/pages/GTMP-ops-degradation-framework
- Related JIRA: GTMP-482 (policy-driven routing enhancements)

Draft status: this is a working brief intended to feed collateral and a sales cheat sheet. Feedback welcome; priority is clarity and reproducibility for reps and CS during incidents.
